title: "Convenience Store Woman: A Life That Fits, Even When It Doesn't Fit In"
author: "Anjali"

description: "My reading of Sayaka Murata's novel about a woman who is content with her life, and a society that refuses to believe her."

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Book:** *Convenience Store Woman* by Sayaka Murata, translated from the Japanese by Ginny Tapley Takemori
:::

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
This review discusses the ending of the book.
:::

I feel every book is written, and read, from a different perspective. The author brings one set of eyes to the story, and each reader brings another. So what follows is not *the* meaning of *Convenience Store Woman*, but what it meant to me.

## The woman behind the counter

At its heart, this is the story of Keiko Furukura, a woman who has worked at the same convenience store since the day it opened. Keiko sees the world from an altogether different angle than the people around her. Things that would upset or excite most people barely touch her. The store, with its routines, its scripted greetings and its manual for how to behave, gives her something the outside world never did: a clear sense of what she is supposed to do and who she is supposed to be.

Nothing in the store bothers her to the point of anger. She is calm and efficient, and she understands the rhythm of the place almost as if she were part of the building itself.

## Borrowing feelings to belong

What struck me most is how Keiko fits in. When her coworkers are annoyed about something, she joins in and echoes their irritation, not because she feels it herself, but because sharing it makes her one of them. She picks up the way they speak and the way they carry themselves, copying their gestures and tone.

It would be easy to read this as emptiness, but I read it differently. For Keiko, mirroring the people around her is how she makes sure she has a say, how she becomes part of the group rather than someone standing outside it. It is a quiet and very human strategy, and it made me think about how much all of us borrow from the people we spend our days with.

## A satisfied woman that society won't believe

The book is also about the life of a single woman who has never married and who is genuinely satisfied with her work. That satisfaction is exactly what the people around her cannot accept. Family, friends and acquaintances keep asking when she will get married or find a "proper" job. Her contentment is never recognised as a valid answer; it is treated as a problem waiting to be fixed.

Again and again, society tries to steer her towards the so-called normal way of living. The pressure is rarely cruel on the surface. It comes as concern, as curiosity, as well-meaning advice. But its weight is constant, and Murata makes you feel how exhausting it is to be questioned about a life you are perfectly happy living.

## Trying to be "normal"

Eventually, Keiko tries to change herself to ease that burden. She lets a man named Shiraha, a bitter former coworker, live in her apartment, because the people around her are suddenly delighted that she seems to have a partner. She even leaves the store and begins preparing for a more respectable job.

For a while, the questions stop. But in giving the world what it wants, Keiko slowly loses the one thing that made her feel alive and certain of herself.

## The calling

In the end, her true calling calls her back. Walking into a convenience store on her way to a job interview, she instinctively senses what the store needs, from the shelves to the displays, and understands that this is who she is. She decides to return to work, at a new convenience store, on her own terms.

It is a strange and wonderful ending, because it is not a story of someone escaping a small life. It is a story of someone refusing to let others define what a full life looks like.

## My takeaway

*Convenience Store Woman* is a short book, but it raises a big question: who gets to decide whether a life is fulfilling? Keiko's life looks small from the outside, yet she is one of the most certain characters I have read about. The book left me thinking about how often we measure other people's happiness against a template, and how much quiet pressure we put on those who simply want something different.

I would recommend it to anyone who has ever felt asked to explain a choice that already made them happy.
